The Pits
thuh PITS
noun (Boomer slang)
From pit (Old English pytt, Latin puteus, a well or hole). The pits, meaning the very worst, is American slang recorded from the 1950s and very common from the late 1960s and 1970s ("This job is the pits"); its origin is debated — perhaps the bottom of a pit, perhaps a shortening of armpits, perhaps the orchestra pit or a cockpit. Older senses survive in the pit as a name for hell and the pits at a racetrack.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The pits means the worst — the bottom, the most miserable situation imaginable. "Being grounded over spring break is the pits." The Christian observation: Scripture knows the pit far better than the slang does, and it knows the way out. The pit in the Bible is the place of the lowest humiliation and danger. Joseph’s brothers "took him, and cast him into a pit: and the pit was empty, there was no water in it" (Gen 37:24). Jeremiah was let down into a cistern where "there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire" (Jer 38:6). And the pit is a name for death and the grave itself: "thou hast kept me alive, that I should not go down to the pit" (Psa 30:3). But the pit is never the last word for God’s people. David’s testimony is the testimony of every saved sinner: "He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings" (Psa 40:2). Joseph went from the pit to the palace. Jeremiah was drawn up by an Ethiopian with old rags and ropes. The Lord Jesus went down into the deepest pit of all, death itself, and came up again. A child who says his day was the pits can be taught, kindly, that he has not yet seen the pit — and that the God of Psalm 40 has never yet lost anyone in one.

Webster 1828 Definition

Boomer-era slang (1950s; common from the late 1960s) for the very worst situation — a light echo of the biblical pit of humiliation and death, out of which the LORD brings His people and sets their feet upon a rock (Psa 40:2).

THE PITS, n. pl. (Boomer slang, 1950s–present) The worst possible situation, place, or thing; something extremely unpleasant. "Monday mornings are the pits."

Webster (1828) — PIT, n. 1. An artificial cavity made in the earth, narrow compared with its depth; distinguished from a well in being generally larger. 2. A deep place; an abyss; profundity. 3. The grave. 4. The shaft of a mine.

Decode for families: one of the most durable Boomer words; your children understand it without translation.

Key Scripture

Psa 40:2 — "He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings."

Gen 37:24 — "And they took him, and cast him into a pit: and the pit was empty, there was no water in it."

Jer 38:6 — "Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire."

Psa 30:3 — "O LORD, thou hast brought up my soul from the grave: thou hast kept me alive, that I should not go down to the pit."

Pro 26:27 — "Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him."

Modern Corruption

A harmless exaggeration in everyday speech; Scripture fills the word with real depth — the pit of humiliation, death, and the grave — and with the real rescue of the God who draws His people up.

expand to see more

The slang trivializes a weighty word, as slang does. Most things called "the pits" are inconveniences. That is not a sin, but it is worth noticing, because a generation that calls a cancelled concert "the pits" has little vocabulary left for genuine affliction. Scripture’s pit is a dry cistern with a boy in it, sold by his brothers; a prophet sinking in mud; the mouth of the grave.

Proverbs adds a moral note: "Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein" (Pro 26:27). Many of the pits we fall into are ones we dug. But even those are not beyond the reach of the God who "brought me up also out of an horrible pit" (Psa 40:2). The gospel is the story of a rescue from the lowest place, by One who went down there Himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin puteus (a well) → Old English pytt → English pit; 1950s–70s American slang the pits (the worst).

expand to see more

Latin puteus — a well, a pit, a shaft

Old English pytt — a hole in the ground; a grave

Hebrew bor — a cistern, a dungeon, the grave (Gen 37:24; Psa 40:2)

1950s American slang: the pits — the worst (origin debated)

Late 1960s–70s: common in everyday speech

Usage

""Losing the game in the last second was the pits.""

"He brought me up also out of an horrible pit (Psa 40:2)."

"Joseph’s pit was the road to the palace (Gen 37:24)."
